summaryEn: The world's largest bicycle maker (the Giant brand) — a global cycling champion now grinding through a deep post-pandemic downturn, loss-making and trading below book value as it waits for the cycle to turn.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + Wikipedia EN/ZH + news; honest cyclical-trough framing)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Giant Manufacturing (TWSE: 9921) is the **world's largest bicycle designer and manufacturer** — the company behind the **Giant** brand (plus Liv for women, Momentum for city riders, and Cadex components), as well as a contract manufacturer for other labels. Founded in **1972** by **King Liu (劉金標)** in Dajia, Taichung, it grew from an OEM supplier into the dominant global cycling brand.

Right now, though, Giant is a **cyclical business at a trough**. After the pandemic cycling boom of 2020–21, the industry suffered a brutal **channel-inventory glut**, and Giant's earnings have yet to fully recover — it posted a **net loss in Q1 2026** (EPS of **-NT$0.51**, a slightly negative net margin) on a still-thin **~19.6% gross margin**. The annual dividend has been **cut sharply, from NT$10 (2021) to NT$2.2 (2024)**, and the shares trade around NT$74 — well below their pandemic-era peak and **below book value (P/B ~0.85)**.

The reported **~185× P/E is not a sign of an expensive stock — it is a trough artifact** of near-zero earnings; the meaningful read for a cyclical at a low is **price-to-book (~0.85)**. The investment question is therefore not "growth," but **whether and when the cycle turns** for the global bicycle leader.

Giant was founded in **1972** in **Dajia, Taichung**, by **King Liu (劉金標)** and partners — initially as a contract manufacturer. The turning point came in **1977**, when Giant struck an **OEM deal with America's Schwinn**, learning to build bicycles at scale for the world's biggest brands.

Liu's ambition, though, was to build a brand of Giant's own. In **1981** the company launched **"Giant" (捷安特)**, and over the following decades turned it into the **world's largest bicycle maker** — adding **Liv** (a women-specific brand, established in 2008 by Bonnie Tu) and **Momentum** (city/commuter, 2010), and building factories across **Taiwan, China, the Netherlands, Hungary and Vietnam**.

King Liu — often called the **"father of Taiwan's bicycle industry"** — handed the chairmanship to **Bonnie Tu (杜綉珍)**, the long-serving finance chief and "godmother of cycling," in 2017, and **reportedly passed away in early 2026**. Under Tu, Giant remains the global brand leader, now navigating the toughest demand environment in its modern history.

- **1972** — Founded in Dajia, Taichung, by King Liu and partners, initially as an OEM.
- **1977** — Signs an OEM deal with Schwinn, scaling its manufacturing.
- **1981** — Launches its own brand, "Giant" (捷安特).
- **1994** — Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (December; ticker 9921).
- **2008** — Bonnie Tu establishes Liv, a women-specific bicycle brand.
- **2010** — Launches Momentum, a city/commuter brand.
- **2017** — King Liu hands the chairmanship to Bonnie Tu.
- **2020–21** — Pandemic cycling boom; record demand and profits.
- **2022–24** — Severe channel-inventory destocking; sales, profits and the dividend fall sharply.
- **2026** — Still loss-making at the start of the year; founder King Liu reportedly passes away.

Giant is a **1972-founded, exchange-listed company — not a venture-backed startup — so it has no seed or Series A/B/C rounds.** It grew from founder capital and OEM contracts into a branded global manufacturer.

## Listing
Giant **listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange in December 1994** (ticker 9921) — a milestone reached while Bonnie Tu was finance chief.

## A balance sheet under cyclical strain
Giant carries a **moderate ~48% debt ratio** on **NT$72bn of total assets** (Q1 2026), against NT$37bn of equity. That leverage is manageable in good times but less comfortable through a downturn that has pushed the company to a **near-break-even/loss position** — TTM return on equity is only about **1%**, versus the mid-teens it earned at the peak.

## A dividend that follows the cycle
Giant's dividend is **not defensive — it tracks earnings**, which is exactly what a cyclical should expect: the cash payout fell from **NT$10/share (2021 peak) to NT$2.2 (2024)** as profits collapsed. The shares now trade **below book value (P/B ~0.85)**; the headline ~185× P/E is meaningless at a trough and should be ignored in favour of book value and through-cycle earnings power.

> *Note: figures on this page are computed on a consolidated basis; the P/E is distorted by near-zero trough earnings. Undocumented historical capital changes are omitted rather than estimated.*

## Core stance: a cyclical-turnaround bet on the global cycling leader, not a growth story

Giant is the **world's #1 bicycle brand** trading **below book value** in the depths of a downturn. The case here is **mean-reversion and franchise durability**, not earnings growth — and it carries real risk because the company is currently **loss-making**.

## Three supporting arguments

**1. An unmatched global franchise.** Giant is the **world's largest bicycle designer and manufacturer**, with the strongest brand portfolio (Giant, Liv, Momentum), a global factory base and an OEM business. Downturns hurt, but they rarely dislodge the category leader.

**2. A trough valuation.** At **~0.85× book** and a dividend that has already been cut to NT$2.2, much of the bad news is in the price. Cyclicals are typically cheapest on through-cycle earnings precisely when current earnings are worst.

**3. A structural tailwind in e-bikes.** Electric bikes have been a growing share of sales (around 30% as far back as 2021) and carry higher value — a genuine, multi-year mix-shift that can lift through-cycle margins.

## The biggest counter-argument

> There is no confirmed bottom. Giant is **still loss-making in early 2026**, the inventory recovery has been stop-start, and a weak consumer or another destocking leg would deepen the losses. This is a turnaround bet on timing — the most honest rebuttal is simply that the cycle has not yet turned.

Giant runs a **dual model**: it sells its **own brands** (Giant, Liv, Momentum) at a brand premium, and it also **manufactures bicycles for other labels (OEM)** — the business it started with in the 1970s.

## Where the money is made
- **Brand + scale.** Owning the world's leading bicycle brand and the largest manufacturing base gives Giant pricing, distribution and cost advantages over smaller rivals.
- **Mix toward e-bikes and premium.** Higher-value electric and performance bikes lift the average selling price and, through the cycle, the margin — a gross margin that runs around the high-teens to low-20s%.
- **Global manufacturing footprint.** Factories in Taiwan, China, the Netherlands, Hungary and Vietnam let Giant serve regional markets and manage tariffs and logistics.

## The cyclical reality
The flip side is that Giant sells a **discretionary consumer durable through a retail channel** — which means it lives and dies by the **inventory cycle**. The pandemic boom pulled demand forward; the 2022–24 destocking then crushed orders and margins. The model's quality is real, but its earnings are inherently volatile.

## A consolidated but deeply cyclical industry

The global bicycle industry is led by a few large players, with Giant the clear #1 by scale. Key competitors include **Merida (美利達, Taiwan's #2)**, and Western brands such as **Trek and Specialized**; Giant also competes with — and manufactures for — many of them.

## The defining dynamic: the inventory cycle
The industry's recent history is dominated by one thing: the **pandemic boom and bust**.
| Phase | What happened |
|---|---|
| 2020–21 | Cycling boom; retailers over-ordered; record sales and profits |
| 2022–24 | Massive channel destocking; orders and margins collapsed industry-wide |
| 2025–26 | Stop-start recovery; Giant still posting losses in early 2026 |

## Where the structural growth is
Beyond the cycle, the durable shift is to **e-bikes and premium/performance bikes**, which carry higher prices and margins. Giant's scale in e-bike production and its brand strength are its best tools to come out of the downturn stronger than smaller competitors.

**Strengths**
- World's largest bicycle designer and manufacturer; strongest brand portfolio (Giant, Liv, Momentum)
- Global manufacturing base (Taiwan, China, Netherlands, Hungary, Vietnam) plus an OEM business
- Structural e-bike mix-shift toward higher-value products

**Weaknesses**
- Currently loss-making (Q1 2026 net loss); TTM ROE only ~1%
- Earnings and dividend are highly cyclical (dividend cut from NT$10 to NT$2.2)
- Discretionary product exposed to the retail inventory cycle

**Opportunities**
- E-bike and premium growth lifting through-cycle margins
- A genuine demand/inventory recovery as the cycle turns
- Trough valuation (below book) if the franchise mean-reverts

**Threats**
- A prolonged or double-dip downturn with no confirmed bottom
- Weak discretionary consumer spending
- Competition and tariff/trade shifts across its global markets

1. **No confirmed cycle bottom** — Giant is still loss-making in early 2026; if demand stays weak or destocking resumes, losses deepen. The single most important variable.
2. **Discretionary demand** — bicycles are a postponable purchase; a soft consumer directly hits volumes.
3. **Inventory whiplash** — the retail channel's over- and under-ordering amplifies Giant's earnings swings.
4. **Leverage through a downturn** — a ~48% debt ratio is manageable in good times but less comfortable while the company is near break-even.
5. **Trade and FX** — tariffs and currency moves across its global factory and sales footprint can swing margins.

Giant's task is to **survive the trough as the franchise leader and let the cycle — and e-bikes — do the rest.** Three things to watch:

**1. The inventory bottom.** The clearest signal will be channel inventory normalising and orders returning to growth. KPI: revenue trend and a return to positive operating margin.

**2. E-bike and premium mix.** The durable margin story is the shift to higher-value electric and performance bikes. KPI: e-bike share of sales and gross-margin recovery.

**3. Through-cycle earnings power.** With the stock below book, the question is what Giant can earn in a normal year — and whether management can defend margins and the balance sheet until then. KPI: ROE recovery toward its historical mid-teens.

**Bottom line.** Giant is the global cycling champion caught in the worst downturn of its modern era — loss-making today, but trading below book with an intact #1 franchise and a real e-bike tailwind. The upside case is a classic cyclical recovery in a category leader; the downside case is that the bottom simply has not arrived yet, and patience (and losses) are required before it does.
